title: U.S. Senate · Wyoming

context.text: This is an open seat: incumbent Cynthia Lummis (R) is not on the November ballot. Harriet Hageman, Wyoming's current at-large U.S. Representative, won the August 18, 2026 Republican primary with 62.2% of the vote. James Byrd, a former state representative, won the Democratic primary with 77.9% of the vote.

candidates.name: Harriet Hageman
candidates.ballotNote: Won the August 18 Republican primary with 62.2% of the vote

summary.text: Harriet Hageman is Wyoming's at-large U.S. Representative, running for the state's open U.S. Senate seat in 2026. A Wyoming attorney for more than three decades, she was elected to the House in 2022 after defeating incumbent Liz Cheney in the Republican primary. She chairs a House Natural Resources subcommittee and serves on the Judiciary Committee.

background.text: Born in Douglas, Wyoming, in 1962. According to her House office, she grew up on a ranch and attended Casper College on a livestock judging scholarship.
Earned a bachelor's degree in business administration (1986) and a law degree (1989) from the University of Wyoming.

Worked as a law clerk for federal appeals judge James E. Barrett, as a lawyer, and as an adjunct professor. Her House biography says she was a litigator for 34 years, admitted to practice before the U.S. Supreme Court.
Co-founded the Wyoming Conservation Alliance and, according to Ballotpedia, was one of the chief litigators opposing the 2001 Roadless Rule.
Ran for Governor of Wyoming in the 2018 Republican primary, finishing third with 21.5% behind Mark Gordon and Foster Friess.
Won the 2022 Republican primary for Wyoming's at-large House seat, defeating incumbent Liz Cheney, and won the general election; re-elected in 2024.

In the 119th Congress, chairs the House Natural Resources Subcommittee on Water, Wildlife, and Fisheries and also serves on its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, on the Judiciary Committee, and as Co-Chair of the Congressional Coal Caucus.
Won the August 18, 2026 Republican primary for U.S. Senate, defeating Samuel Mead and three others, for the seat Sen. Cynthia Lummis is leaving.

positions.summary: Has said she will support laws to protect unborn life and described abortion as a stain on American history.
positions.quote: Abortion will one day be remembered as a grave stain on American history.

positions.summary: Says the political left seeks to dissolve the right to keep and bear arms and that she will fight to protect that right.
positions.quote: They want to eliminate freedom of speech, dissolve our right to keep and bear arms, and seize our private property.

positions.summary: Has criticized federal tax policy as imposing "bone-crushing taxes on American families."
positions.quote: Their agenda is Critical Race Theory, imposing bone-crushing taxes on American families.

record.text: Chairs the House Natural Resources Subcommittee on Water, Wildlife and Fisheries and serves on the House Committee on the Judiciary for the 119th Congress (2025-2026).

candidates.name: James Byrd
candidates.ballotNote: Won the August 18 Democratic primary with 77.9% of the vote
candidates.currentRole: Former member, Wyoming House of Representatives

summary.text: James Byrd is a former Wyoming state representative and professional geophysicist running as the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. A fifth-generation Wyomingite from Cheyenne, he served ten years in the Wyoming House, including as a Democratic leader. He says he is running on an independent approach focused on working families' costs, rural health care, and public lands.

background.text: Describes himself as a fifth-generation Wyomingite; earned a high school diploma from Cheyenne Central High School and attended Laramie County Community College and the University of Wyoming.
His mother, Liz Byrd, was Wyoming's first Black state senator, and his father, Jim Byrd, was the state's first Black police chief, according to his candidate survey.

Worked as a security consultant, computer network designer, exploration geophysicist (including for Compagnie Generale de Geophysique and Amoco/BP), and contract computer project manager for firms including American Express and Cargill.
Served ten years in the Wyoming House of Representatives, District 44, from 2009 to 2019, winning re-election in 2012 and later cycles.

In the legislature, served as Minority Whip from 2013 to 2015 and was elected Minority Caucus Leader in 2015; his committees included Corporations, Elections and Political Subdivisions and Minerals, Business and Economic Development.
Advanced from the 2026 Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, defeating Billy Benavidez.

priorities.text: "Working families are getting hammered by the 'Daily Squeeze'... I'm running to tackle these kitchen-table realities head-on... aggressively protecting our rural healthcare clinics from corporate neglect."

"Keeping public lands in public hands while leading the energy future... I will fiercely protect public access to our lands for hunting, fishing, and outdoor recreation against any federal overreach or corporate sell-off schemes."

"I am deeply focused on rural healthcare infrastructure, energy innovation, and workforce education. Protecting critical access hospitals and community clinics is a matter of survival for our rural towns."

positions.summary: As a Wyoming state representative, voted yes on a floor amendment to the 2015 budget bill (HB 1) that would have set aside state funds for Wyoming's share of expanded Medicaid coverage under the ACA; the amendment failed in the House 15-41.

record.text: Voted yes on a 2015 budget-bill floor amendment (HB0001H3031) that would have set aside state funds for Wyoming's share of expanded Medicaid coverage under the Affordable Care Act; the amendment failed in the House 15-41.

candidates.researchNotes: Completed Ballotpedia's 2026 Candidate Connection survey but responses do not clearly state positions on the guide's fixed issue list. The Medicaid-expansion amendment vote is dated to the House's 2015 general-session budget-bill floor debate (HB 1), but the specific calendar day was not shown on the House Digest of Bills page retrieved, so no date is given.
